summary: This standards-track RFC defines the architecture for IP and LDP fast reroute using maximally redundant trees. It gives link and node protection with full coverage in any topology that remains connected after the failure.

eli5.summary: Each router prepares two different paths to every place, so if one road breaks, traffic switches to the other right away.

questions: fast reroute with maximally redundant trees
what is the default mrt profile
subtitle: How routers pre-compute two maximally separate backup trees so any single link or node failure has a ready detour.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, traffic is lost until the routing protocol reconverges, and earlier fast-reroute methods cannot always find a backup path in every topology.
tldr.mechanism: Each destination gets two Maximally Redundant Trees, MRT-Blue and MRT-Red, that share only links and nodes whose loss would split the network. A router next to a failure moves traffic onto whichever tree avoids it, using LDP labels or IP tunnels.
tldr.outcome: MRT-FRR gives link and node protection with 100% coverage for any single failure that leaves the network connected. This architecture leaves several protocol extensions and the tree algorithm to other documents.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: 100% for single link or node failure if the network stays connected

facts.label: Tree computation cost
facts.value: O(e + n log n), less than three SPFs

facts.label: Proxy-node attachment
facts.value: At most two routers in the island

today: RFC 7812 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the tree algorithm to RFC 7811 and several signaling extensions to other documents.

sections.title: Why Another Fast Reroute Method
sections.content:
RFC 7812 defines the architecture for IP and LDP fast reroute using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR). MRT-FRR creates two alternate forwarding trees that are separate from the primary next-hop forwarding used during stable operation. The two trees are maximally diverse from each other, so they give link and node protection for 100% of paths and failures, as long as the failure does not cut the network into multiple pieces.

Fast reroute rests on the single failure assumption: the time between single failures is long enough for the network to reconverge. Real topologies keep changing through maintenance, costed-out links and new equipment, and methods such as Loop-Free Alternates (LFA) and Remote LFA are sensitive to those changes. A method with guaranteed coverage is therefore valuable. It also lets slower micro-loop prevention schemes such as Ordered FIB or Nearside Tunneling take their time without dropping traffic to unprotected destinations.

The RFC is honest about the costs. MRT does not protect against multiple simultaneous failures and ignores Shared Risk Link Groups. The MRT Lowpoint algorithm is also new, so every MRT router must compute the same thing correctly. The algorithm itself is in RFC 7811, and multicast use is not covered here.
sections.eli5: If a bridge on your route to school closes, it helps to already know a second way to go. MRT-FRR makes every router learn two different ways to reach each place before anything breaks.

sections.title: Maximally Redundant Trees and Fast Reroute
sections.content:
A pair of Maximally Redundant Trees is a pair of directed spanning trees that give maximally disjoint paths toward a common root. Only links or nodes whose failure would partition the network (cut-links and cut-vertices) are shared. In a 2-connected graph the paths are fully link- and node-disjoint. In other graphs they are as disjoint as the topology allows. By convention the two trees are called MRT-Blue and MRT-Red.

Every destination has its own pair of trees, so each router stores its normal primary next hops plus MRT-Blue and MRT-Red next hops toward each destination. The RFC says the tree computation runs in O(e + n log n), less than three SPF runs. MRT-FRR is realized with multi-topology forwarding: one Blue and one Red forwarding topology next to the default one.

Forwarding does not change until a local failure is detected. The appropriate alternate is pre-computed, and RFC 7811 says how to choose between Blue and Red for a given primary next hop. Using an MRT alternate is a local decision, and an operator may prefer an LFA or another alternate instead. Unlike non-downstream LFAs, which RFC 5286 notes can loop on a worse failure than expected, MRT alternates will not cause looping, because traffic already on an MRT is not repaired again by another router.
sections.eli5: Think of a blue road and a red road to the same town that only share the parts you cannot avoid, like a single bridge. If something blocks one road, you take the other one.

sections.title: Forwarding Traffic Along an MRT
sections.content:
Three router roles appear on an MRT path. The MRT ingress router, which is the Point of Local Repair (PLR) in fast reroute, moves a packet off its shortest path. Transit routers keep it on the same MRT. The MRT egress router returns it to shortest-path forwarding. Transit behavior is the same for any traffic type, while ingress and egress depend on whether the packet is LDP or IP.

Four transit mechanisms are considered. Option 1A uses multi-topology LDP from RFC 7307: each FEC gets three topology-scoped labels, one each for the default, Red and Blue topologies. It is simple for hardware but uses more label space and LDP signaling. Option 1B uses a two-label stack, a topology-id label on top of the normal FEC label, which uses fewer labels but makes packets bigger and label operations more complex. Options 2A and 2B tunnel in IPv4 or IPv6 to special MRT-Red and MRT-Blue loopback addresses that each router announces.

For LDP traffic the PLR swaps the usual label for the MRT label of the same FEC, so no tunneling and no targeted LDP sessions are needed. For IP traffic, tunneling is the only practical way to mark the topology, and the RFC chose not to define an IPv6-only solution. Routers implementing MRT fast reroute of LDP traffic MUST support Option 1A, and MPLS routers doing IP MRT fast reroute MUST support tunneling of IP traffic with Option 1A.
sections.eli5: The router can mark a package as taking the blue road or the red road in a few ways, such as a sticker on the package or a bigger envelope around it. Every router on the way reads the mark and keeps the package on that road.

sections.title: MRT Islands and Profiles
sections.content:
Routers must agree on the same options and the same set of nodes and links to build consistent trees. The options are grouped into an MRT Profile, identified by an 8-bit Profile ID. An MRT Island is the set of routers that support the same profile, in the same IGP area or level, joined by bidirectional links. Island formation runs separately for each profile a router advertises, and disconnected islands operate independently.

Existing IGP mechanisms for discouraging traffic are respected. A link MUST be excluded if its cost is 0xFFFFFE (IS-IS) or 0xFFFF (OSPF) in either direction. A router MUST be excluded if it has the IS-IS overload bit set, advertises 0xFFFF on all outgoing OSPF interfaces, or lacks the V6-bit or R-bit in an OSPFv3 Router LSA. Links can also be advertised as MRT-Ineligible, and the protocol extensions for that are left to other documents.

A profile specifies the MRT algorithm, the Red and Blue MPLS MT-IDs, a GADAG root selection policy, the forwarding mechanism, recalculation behavior and area border behavior. This RFC defines only the Default MRT Profile, Profile ID 0: the MRT Lowpoint algorithm of RFC 7811, forwarding Option 1A, and a root chosen as the highest Router ID among routers with the lowest GADAG Root Selection Priority value. Routers can run several profiles side by side, which eases migration to a new profile.

The RFC creates the IANA "MRT Profile Identifier Registry", and the Default MRT Profile is the first entry. LDP signaling extensions, including a special Rainbow MRT MT-ID that stands for all Red and Blue topologies, are left to another document.
sections.eli5: Routers join a club only if they follow the same rulebook, and the club is called an island. Each rulebook has a number, and rulebook number 0 is the one this document writes down.

sections.title: Area Borders and Multihomed Prefixes
sections.content:
When traffic leaves an area, it should also leave the Red or Blue topology and return to shortest-path forwarding. The RFC gives three reasons: the default topology gives the shortest route, a single failure seen in several areas (an ABR failure, for example) can be repaired separately in each, and the packet can be fast-rerouted again if a second distinct failure occurs. With Option 1A, the ABR controls this by what it advertises. To neighbors in the best area it advertises distinct primary, Blue and Red labels. To routers in other areas it advertises the primary label for the default topology and for the Rainbow MRT MT-ID, so packets from there arrive on the default topology. With IP tunneling, the ABR decapsulates a packet whose outer address is its own MRT loopback address.

Prefixes attached to the island in more than one place, and destinations outside the island, need special handling. The RFC describes two approaches. With tunnel endpoint selection, the PLR picks another router attached to the prefix that is loop-free with respect to the failure, and tunnels to it. With a named proxy-node, a stand-in for the prefix is attached to at most two routers in the island, chosen by lowest cost, with ties broken by lowest Router ID. Packets sent to the proxy-node leave the MRT there and go on by shortest path. Proxy-nodes work for LDP traffic without targeted LDP sessions, and they MUST be supported when LDP forwarding is supported and a label binding for the destination is sent to an Island Border Router.

Appendix B points out a limit: a prefix announced in two different non-backbone areas may be impractical to protect without explicit tunneling, and the same is true of LFA and Remote LFA.
sections.eli5: When a package leaves one town for another, it switches back to the normal main road. Where a place has two front doors, the router picks the door that is still safe.

sections.title: Convergence and Recalculation
sections.content:
After a failure, MRT detours carry packets while the IGP reconverges. The RFC discusses how MRT-FRR fits with the micro-loop prevention techniques of RFC 5715. With Nearside Tunneling, traffic relies on the PLR's local repair for longer, so MRT's full coverage makes it an attractive repair path. With Farside Tunneling, the Blue or Red path from a remote upstream router to the destination is guaranteed to avoid a link failure or inferred node failure, and MRT paths cannot be caught in micro-loops because they are locked to the pre-failure topology.

For the Default MRT Profile, recalculation SHOULD follow this order at each router: receive the failure notification, recompute the shortest path tree, install it in the FIB, wait a configured or advertised period for traffic to drain from the MRTs if the network was stable before the failure, recompute the MRTs, and install them. Until the new MRTs are installed, protection coverage is lower, so the RFC says to recalculate and install them quickly.
sections.eli5: After the road is fixed and everyone is using the normal map again, the routers wait until nobody is still on a detour. Only then do they draw new detour maps.

sections.title: Operating MRT-FRR
sections.content:
MRT paths carry no normal traffic, only fast-reroute traffic shortly after a failure. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS proactive monitoring, and implementations SHOULD let operators test MRT paths with OAM traffic, for example MPLS ping and traceroute for topology-scoped FECs.

Backup paths can need different capacity than post-convergence paths, because traffic flows differ during a fast-reroute event. Operators can model this and add capacity or change backup paths. Adjusting IGP metrics is not a generally applicable tool for that, but marking a link MRT-Ineligible keeps backup traffic off it. Policy-based selection can also prefer, say, a downstream LFA over an MRT alternate.

MRT-FRR keeps working when connectivity is degraded: paths stay fully diverse within a block, and shared parts are only cut-links or cut-vertices. In a partial deployment, only routers advertising a profile join the island, and paths to outside destinations are diverse within the island but possibly not outside it. If IP tunneling is used, each router needs unique MRT-Red and MRT-Blue loopback addresses.
sections.eli5: A spare tire is only useful if you check it before the flat. Operators test the backup paths regularly and make sure the backup roads are wide enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MRT forwarding paths do not follow shortest paths, and the forwarding state exists before any failure. A malicious packet with a suitable header injected from a compromised location would be forwarded along a non-shortest path. A network security design should therefore not assume that malicious traffic follows only shortest paths. The RFC notes that non-shortest paths are not unique to MRT.

MRT-FRR also relies on routers advertising information used to build backup paths. False information could steer backup paths over compromised links, and combined with the ability to cause failures that could expose traffic. A receiving router therefore needs to be able to authenticate MRT-related information claimed to come from another router.
sections.eli5: Backup roads are real roads that exist all the time, so a sneaky person could use them too. Routers should also check that the notes about the roads really came from the right router.
